# Fieldguide runbook

Fieldguide is one local system in four processes. Leave the ports and the JSON fields as they are. The retrieval service listens on port 8000. Liveness is GET /health. The body is a status of ok and the number of chunks currently loaded. Search is POST /search. The request carries a query string and a k. The response carries hits. Each hit has an id, the chunk text, and a rerank_score from the second-stage scorer. Clients send that shape. The service loads its indexes once at startup. Rebuilding the chunk file is an offline step. POST /search does not rewrite the corpus.

The token service listens on port 8001. It exposes a chat-completions route whose body is a server-sent event stream. Each event line carries a choice with a delta content string, and the stream

e whose body is a server-sent event stream. Each event line carries a choice with a delta content string, and the stream ends with a done sentinel. The voice process listens on port 8010 at the WebSocket path /ws. The message types for that socket live beside the voice code. The browser page is static and is served on port 5500. These processes bind to loopback. This runbook does not assume a public host.

Assistant answers in the supervised set are short on purpose. A labeled assistant turn is 2-4 sentences. That band is long enough to state the fact and the reason, and short enough that a small model can learn the rhythm. The same band is what we want once a generator is wired to POST /search: ground the reply in a returned hit, then stop. A hit should not be padded into a long essay,

r is wired to POST /search: ground the reply in a returned hit, then stop. A hit should not be padded into a long essay, and a question that asks for a reason should not come back as a single noun phrase. The 2-4 sentences rule is the writing rule for labeled rows and the reading rule for anyone judging a generation. Count sentences, and keep the character length of those rows inside the band the validator will enforce later.

The corpus behind the retrieval service is three markdown notes, cut into character windows, and stored as JSON lines. An id is a filename stem, a colon, and a zero-based index. Hybrid search keeps a dense index and a lexical index on those same ids, then fuses the two rankings. Reciprocal rank fusion uses a constant k of 60. The score added for a list is one

same ids, then fuses the two rankings. Reciprocal rank fusion uses a constant k of 60. The score added for a list is one divided by k plus the rank, and ranks start at 1. A document missing from one list does not receive a term from that list. Ties break by id. That constant is a rank smoother. It is not a cosine, and it is not the k on POST /search. The request k is how many hits to return. The fusion k only shapes the combined rank score.

Run the retrieval code from its own virtualenv. The fine-tune environment and the speech environment are separate, because those dependency sets do not solve cleanly together. Model weights, adapters, and the vector index stay on disk and out of git. Notes, JSON lines, and metric files stay in the tree. If a download asks for a Hugging Face login, the

k and out of git. Notes, JSON lines, and metric files stay in the tree. If a download asks for a Hugging Face login, the token stays in the local credential store and never in a committed file. A blank metric stays blank until the command has been run. Copy the number from the terminal. Do not refill it from memory on a later day.

A healthy retrieval check looks like this. GET /health returns ok and a chunk count that matches the JSON lines file. POST /search for a question these notes can answer returns a hit whose id prefix is the note that contains the fact, and the hit text actually contains that fact. Latency and recall belong in the eval folder as JSON before they are copied into the activity log. When a job later rebuilds the index, a failed job must leave the previous chunk file

y are copied into the activity log. When a job later rebuilds the index, a failed job must leave the previous chunk file and the previous index in place. A path that escapes the raw notes directory is a failed job, not a search.

# Fine-tuning with mlx_lm.lora and QLoRA

Local fine-tuning on this machine goes through MLX. The command is mlx_lm.lora. It trains a low-rank adapter on top of a frozen language model. LoRA leaves the base matrix where it is and learns a pair of small matrices whose product is the update. You store the adapter, not a second full copy of the network. Rank is the width of that update. A later comparison in this project changes rank and leaves the data, the seed, and the step count alone, so a loss gap can be attributed to rank.

QLoRA is that same adapter story with a quantized base. The base weights stay in low bit width, here a 4-bit checkpoint, and the adapter matrices stay in higher precision so the optimizer has a stable update. mlx_lm.lora takes the QLoRA path when the checkpoint you

stay in higher precision so the optimizer has a stable update. mlx_lm.lora takes the QLoRA path when the checkpoint you pass is already quantized. Point the same command at a full-precision model and the run is ordinary LoRA. This project does not quantize inside the training loop. It downloads an already quantized instruct model, which is why the run is QLoRA without a separate conversion step. The checkpoint we train is a 4-bit Llama 3.2 instruct model around one billion parameters. If a license gate blocks that download, the swap is a 4-bit Qwen 2.5 instruct model at about half a billion parameters, and the hyperparameters stay put. The swap, if it happens, is written down. The token used to accept a license stays outside the repo.

The data argument is a directory, not a single file.

The data argument is a directory, not a single file. For a training run the loader requires train.jsonl. If valid.jsonl is in that directory, mlx_lm.lora reports validation loss during the run. test.jsonl is the file evaluate mode reads when the test flag is set. We keep all three. train.jsonl supplies the updates. valid.jsonl puts a validation loss in the log. test.jsonl stays held out for perplexity after training. Each line is one JSON object, and a single example must not be split across lines. The chat shape is a messages list: a user turn, then an assistant turn, each with a role and content. A prompt-plus-completion line and a raw text line are also legal shapes. This set uses chat so the model's own chat template

ompt-plus-completion line and a raw text line are also legal shapes. This set uses chat so the model's own chat template can wrap the turns. Keys the loader does not expect are ignored, so labels hidden in extra fields will not enter the loss.

A few flags dominate when memory is tight. The documented default batch size is 4. This project uses one sequence at a time. The number of layers that receive adapters can be reduced, which shrinks the backward pass, and that cut is the documented response to an out-of-memory error. Sequence length is capped so one long note cannot blow the activation memory. Prompt masking, when it is on, drops the user tokens out of the loss and trains on the assistant span. For chat data the final message is the completion. The iteration count is a fixed budget,

trains on the assistant span. For chat data the final message is the completion. The iteration count is a fixed budget, not an epoch count, so a small hand-written set still finishes in one sitting. Two hundred steps will not support a claim about which rank is universally better. They will show whether the loss moved, and whether rank 16 moved it differently from rank 8.

The adapter directory is the artifact. Learned weights land on disk and stay out of git. A resume points at the saved adapter file. Fusing the adapter back into the base is a separate command and is not part of the training log. What the log must contain is the iteration losses, so a parser can read the first train loss, the last train loss, and the last validation loss when valid.jsonl was present. The same data

read the first train loss, the last train loss, and the last validation loss when valid.jsonl was present. The same data directory, the same seed, and the same flags are reused when the second run changes rank. If the command line and the YAML disagree, the command line wins, which is a reason to write the exact invocation next to the log.

Training stays on the host. A container on this plan does not expose Metal, so mlx_lm.lora is not something we expect to run inside that image. The quantized base plus the higher-precision adapter is the QLoRA setup the MLX guide describes, and the three files train.jsonl, valid.jsonl, and test.jsonl are the whole supervised set.

The ingest worker does not patch the live index in place. It rebuilds every note in data/raw, writes the next dense and lexical indexes into a sibling directory, and only then publishes that directory. That publish is an atomic index swap: the new directory replaces the live one after the build has succeeded. A failed build leaves the previous index where search already found it.

The same rebuild reads the directory, not a single file. Ingesting one note a second time adds nothing, because the chunk ids come from the file name and the window index. A path that climbs out of data/raw with a parent segment is rejected before any of those files change. The job record then says the attempt failed, and the chunk list stays as it was.

Search keeps serving the old index until the directory

Search keeps serving the old index until the directory mtime changes. The API notices that change and loads the swapped files. The queue can retry the job, and max_tries stays at two, but a retry still rebuilds from the directory rather than appending a second copy of the note. The live directory is the one a search reads. The next directory is disposable until that swap succeeds.

# Retrieval: bi-encoder, cross-encoder, and Recall@k

A retrieval-augmented model answers from two memories. One memory sits in the weights. The other is a corpus you can edit, re-chunk, and re-index without another training run. Lewis and colleagues describe that system as a retriever plus a generator. The retriever selects passages. The generator writes while those passages are in view. This folder is the corpus side of that split. Chunk ids have to stay fixed, because every later number, from a similarity score to Recall@k, names one of them.

The first retriever in this stack is a bi-encoder. A bi-encoder pushes the query through a transformer and pushes each passage through the same transformer on its own. Each call returns a single vector. The passage call does not see the query, so

through the same transformer on its own. Each call returns a single vector. The passage call does not see the query, so those vectors can be computed once, L2-normalized, and stored. After normalization, cosine similarity is an inner product, and a flat index can scan it by brute force while the collection is small. That independence is the operational point of a bi-encoder: the expensive passage encoding happens offline, and a new question encodes only the query.

Independence is also the limit. Tokens in the query never attend to tokens in the passage, so a near paraphrase can outrank the sentence that actually answers the question. A second model repairs the order. A cross-encoder scores a pair. You pack the query and one passage into one sequence. Self-attention then mixes the two

. A cross-encoder scores a pair. You pack the query and one passage into one sequence. Self-attention then mixes the two sides, and the network emits one relevance number for that pair rather than a vector you could file in an index. Change the query and every score is invalid. The passage encoding is not reusable across queries, which is why a cross-encoder is the wrong object to precompute.

The cost of that joint forward pass is why the cross-encoder runs on a shortlist. A retrieve step, the bi-encoder or a lexical index or both, nominates a few dozen chunks. The second stage is a re-rank: the cross-encoder scores only those candidates and the caller keeps the new top of the list. In the pipeline this corpus is for, the shortlist is about twenty fused hits and the cross-encoder keeps

op of the list. In the pipeline this corpus is for, the shortlist is about twenty fused hits and the cross-encoder keeps five. Scoring every chunk would repeat a full pairwise pass per chunk. That is the wrong shape for interactive search even when the collection is only a handful of notes. The shortlist is the stage where the pair model stays affordable.

Recall@k checks the first stage, not the taste of the re-rank. It is 1 when a labeled chunk id shows up anywhere in the top k, and 0 when it does not. A re-rank can move a relevant id upward inside the list it was given. It cannot recover an id the retriever dropped. If Recall@k is 0 on the shortlist, the cross-encoder never sees the right text, and the final list stays wrong. That is why Recall@k is logged on the bi-encoder, on the

oder never sees the right text, and the final list stays wrong. That is why Recall@k is logged on the bi-encoder, on the lexical list, and on the fused list before anyone celebrates a prettier order.

The windows in this corpus are character spans. The default width is 800 characters with an overlap of 120. The end of a window snaps back to a space in the last 80 characters when one exists, so a cut prefers a word boundary. Overlap keeps a sentence that straddles a cut inside two neighboring chunks. The id is the filename stem, a colon, and the window index starting at 0. `retrieval-notes:0` has to mean the same string after a rebuild, or a later labeled set becomes a guess. Overlap must be smaller than the window. An empty note contributes no rows.

guess. Overlap must be smaller than the window. An empty note contributes no rows.

Passage vectors from the bi-encoder are what the local dense index stores. Query vectors are the only ones computed at search time. The cross-encoder never writes those vectors. It only re-scores pairs that the earlier stage already returned. Keep that order straight when a latency number shows up: embedding the corpus is a one-time cost, and the pair model is a per-query cost on a short list.
